content: " The article critiques the enduring, yet fundamentally flawed, 19th-century ‘Great Man’ theory of history—a deterministic worldview popularized by Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle, who argued that exceptional individuals—such as Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and the prophet Muhammad—single-handedly shape human destiny through their superior intellect, charisma, and willpower. According to Carlyle, ordinary people play a passive, subordinate role: merely observing, admiring, and obediently following these heroic figures in what he termed ‘universal history’. Though this top-down, elitist conception has been robustly challenged by egalitarian thought, Marxist analyses emphasizing class struggle, and especially by E.P. Thompson’s influential 1960s ‘history from below’—which centers the agency, resistance, and lived experiences of marginalized, everyday people—the Great Man myth remains culturally resilient and dangerously seductive. The piece observes that the belief in heroic, divinely or naturally ordained leadership continues to attract individuals—predominantly men—who cultivate self-mythologies of exceptionalism, destiny, and moral superiority. These figures often frame their ambition as a sacred duty or messianic calling, claiming unparalleled insight and the right to impose their vision unilaterally. However, rather than embodying the traditional virtues associated with heroism—such as humility, empathy, sacrifice, and service—the modern incarnations of Carlyle’s ‘great men’ are frequently authoritarian, ruthless, arrogant, and contemptuous of democratic norms and collective wisdom. Consequently, the article contends that far from being heroic saviors, such leaders function more accurately as anti-heroes or outright villains—wielding immense power not to liberate or uplift, but to dominate, manipulate, and consolidate control at the expense of pluralism, justice, and human dignity. The persistence of this ideology, the text warns, poses a profound threat to democratic societies and historical understanding alike."
